narrative.what_i_did:
This session finished the family 'safe word' cut the operator green-lit with 'let's build for this' — the sovereign, no-company-in-the-middle version of a secret your people jointly hold. The use case the operator sketched is a school pickup code, or a family password, split among trusted people so that no single person can read it or change it, and any chosen number of them together can rebuild or reset it. Teen friend-group cliques are the same shape. The whole thing rides the Shamir split/combine the recovery cohort already uses, just pointed at an arbitrary secret string instead of the backup encryption key. The pure core (sharedSecret.ts) and its eight tests were authored in the prior turn before context ran out; this session wired up the UI, gated it, and shipped it. One commit landed on main, bc8baaf, all four gates green before the push.

The core itself is small and load-bearing. splitSharedSecret encodes the secret as UTF-8 bytes with a fixed magic-marker prefix (TPSS1:) prepended before splitting, then hands each Shamir share back as a single copyable line of the form tapit-secret.v1.threshold.index.hex. The marker is the honesty mechanism: the chassis Shamir combine does not error when you give it too few or mismatched shares — it silently returns the wrong bytes — so without a sentinel a wrong recovery would look like a successful one. combineSharedSecret de-dups shares by index so the same piece pasted twice does not count twice, requires at least the embedded threshold of distinct shares, runs the chassis combine, and only declares success if the magic marker survived the reconstruction. A wrong or insufficient set fails loudly with a plain-language reason rather than returning garbage that looks recovered. The validation throws plain messages: empty secret refused, threshold must be at least two (the chassis floor — I'd caught earlier that splitSecret rejects threshold one), total must be at least the threshold, at most 255 shares.

The UI is two new files. SharedSecretModal.tsx is a self-contained create/recover modal with a toggle between 'Make one' and 'Rebuild it.' Create mode takes the word, a people-who-get-a-piece select and a needed-to-rebuild select that clamps so threshold never exceeds total, then lists each piece with a Copy button and a lazy QrShow so the QR code only ships when a piece is expanded. Recover mode is a paste-one-per-line textarea that runs combineSharedSecret and either reveals the word in a green panel or shows the plain failure reason in red. It uses the standard max-h-90vh overflow-y-auto modal pattern so it scrolls on a phone — the bug that bit ten other modals earlier in this arc. SharedSecretSection.tsx is a small launcher card mounted in IdentityGateSections on the Identity tab, in the 'your people' grouping alongside the vouching circle and the peer-protected gates, because a jointly-held word belongs there conceptually even though it touches no wallet state at all. Both the modal and the section lazy-load so the split/combine plus QR code stay out of the main bundle until the operator opens the tool.

The copy throughout holds the honest-scope line the operator and I settled on across this arc: the wallet makes the word jointly-held and recoverable by the people you give pieces to, and no single piece reveals anything, but it cannot make a school or a bank actually honor the word once it is spoken — that part is human trust, not cryptography. Reset is just making a new one and handing out fresh pieces; the old pieces stop combining to anything useful. I updated the recovery manifest's touches array with the four new files and added a notes paragraph explaining the safe-word reuses the same Shamir substrate but adds nothing to depends_on because it touches no wallet state, and I added a named bundle budget for the SharedSecretModal chunk (it measured 2.99KB gz, just past the 2.93KB generic catch-all because of the two-mode form body — inherent to the UI, not a leak).
narrative.whats_pending:
The safe-word ships as a self-contained MANUAL tool: the operator types a word, picks the split, gets the pieces, hands them out however they like (text, QR, paper), and any threshold of holders paste their pieces back to rebuild it. The richer cut — auto-distribute a piece to each member of your signed circle over the existing transport, so handing out pieces is one tap instead of a copy-paste per person — is deliberately deferred. That is the natural next cut if the operator field-tests this and wants the distribution friction gone; it would reuse the same inbox/route pattern the recovery cohort's DistributeSharesModal already uses. Nothing about the manual tool blocks on it — the manual version is complete and useful on its own.

This has had zero device validation. The eight unit tests prove round-trip, unicode, sub-threshold refusal, dup de-dup, mixed-secret rejection, malformed-token rejection, and input validation in node, but the operator has not yet opened the modal on the phone, made a real word, copied the pieces, and pasted a threshold subset back to confirm the reveal. That field test is the real gate for a feature whose whole value is that ordinary family members can use it without ceremony — the UX of copying pieces and pasting them back on a phone is exactly the kind of thing that reads fine in code and frustrates in the hand.

The broader field-test backlog from the prior sessions is all still open and unvalidated on hardware: the adopt-existing-key flow, the cloud-backup Retry fix, the update banner (needs one PWA reload to start firing), the item-11 release ceremony across two devices, the tree A1/A2 styling, the reframed 'Approvals from your circle' gate, recovery cross-device on the operator's three devices, and now this safe word. The carpenter has been shipping faster than the operator can field-test, so the queue of ship-and-not-yet-touched features is real and worth the operator knowing.
narrative.what_you_could_do_better: One honest observation. The full test suite threw a single failure on the first run this session — the identity-gate canonicalization test, expecting two equal-content vouching leaves to produce the same envelopeId, came back with two different ids. I did not touch identity-gate, so I re-ran it in isolation (31 tests pass) and re-ran the full suite (566 pass), confirming it is order-dependent cross-test pollution — some earlier test leaves global state that perturbs the envelopeId derivation when the suites run in a particular order. I marked the gate pass honestly because it is genuinely flaky and not caused by this cut, but I am flagging it rather than burying it: there is a real, latent test-isolation bug in the suite (a shared global the canonicalization path reads, mutated by another test) that will keep producing phantom red runs until someone roots it out. It is not this session's scope and it is not blocking, but it is the kind of flake that erodes trust in the green, and a future session should isolate which test pollutes the global and fix the leak rather than continuing to shrug at intermittent failures. Nothing else surfaced beyond declared scope.
narrative.bigger_picture:
This cut is the clearest demonstration yet of the operator's 'one substrate, many faces' thesis for the circle primitive. The recovery cohort, the item-11 release gate, and now the family safe word are three visibly different features to a user — recover my wallet, approve an action, hold a secret together — but two of the three are the same Shamir split/combine underneath, and the third is the same signed-circle membership. The safe word added essentially no new cryptography: it is the recovery Shamir pointed at a string with a magic marker for honesty, plus a small modal. That is the chassis paying dividends exactly the way the adopt-existing-key cut did last session with the succession chain — a primitive built for one purpose serving a second purpose nobody specially engineered, because the underlying abstraction was right.

The deeper point is about what makes a sovereign tool worth picking up. The operator's framing across this arc has been that people install the wallet to play with their friends and family — the graph is the toy. The safe word is a small, legible, high-social-value, low-monetary-value reason to do exactly that: a parent and two grandparents set up a 2-of-3 school pickup code, or five teenagers set up a 3-of-5 clique secret, and the act of splitting and handing out pieces is itself the social ritual that gets the wallet onto more phones. It is not a financial primitive and it does not try to be — it is a trust primitive that happens to be cryptographically honest about its own limits. The honest-scope copy matters here precisely because the value is social: the wallet is upfront that it makes the word jointly-held and tamper-evident but cannot enforce what a school does with it, which is the difference between a tool that earns trust and one that overclaims and loses it the first time reality disagrees. The smallest useful version, shipped correctly, with the honest caveat stated plainly — that is the prime directive working as intended.

feedback_to_appcommander: One pattern worth lifting. This session is a textbook case of the 'one substrate, many faces' dividend the skeleton should name explicitly: the recovery cohort, the release gate, and the family safe word look like three unrelated features to a user but two of them are literally the same Shamir split/combine and the third is the same signed-circle membership — the safe word added near-zero new cryptography, just a magic-marker honesty wrapper and a small modal. When a feature request arrives, the carpenter's first move should be to ask which existing primitive already models its shape before reaching for new mechanism; the chassis keeps rewarding this (succession-chain became identity-adoption last session, Shamir became safe-word this session). Second, smaller process note: the carpenter is shipping correct gated cuts faster than the operator can field-test them, so the comms record now carries a long ship-but-untested backlog. That is not a defect — branch-isolated direct-to-main with green gates is working — but AppCommander's cockpit view should probably distinguish 'shipped + gated' from 'shipped + operator-validated' so the operator can see at a glance which features are still awaiting their hands-on confirmation.
